{{short description|Table using constrained sand for modelling or educational purposes}}
{{redirect|Abax|the ground beetle genus|Abax (beetle)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2021}}

A '''sand table''', or '''sandboard''', uses constrained sand for writing, modelling, or educational purposes. The original version of a sand table may be the {{tlit|grc|abax}} used by early Greek students. They were later used throughout the [[Arab world]]. In the modern era, one common use for a sand table is to make terrain models for [[military plan]]ning and [[wargaming]].

== Abax ==
[[File:Abax from Darius Vase.jpg|thumb|{{tlit|grc|Abax}} depicted on the [[Darius Vase]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Williams |first=Michael R. |title=A history of computing technology |date=1998 |publisher=IEEE Computer Soc. |location=Los Alamitos, CA |isbn=978-0-8186-7739-7 |page=56 |edition=Second}}</ref>]]

An {{tlit|grc|abax}} ({{lang|grc|ἄβαξ}}) was a table covered with sand commonly used by students, particularly in Greece, to perform studies such as writing, geometry, and calculations.{{sfn|Smith|1958|p=177–178}}

The {{tlit|grc|abax}} was the predecessor to the [[abacus]]. Objects, such as stones, were added for counting and then columns for [[place-value]] arithmetic. The demarcation between an {{tlit|grc|abax}} and an abacus seems to be poorly defined in history;{{sfn|Ifrah|2000|p=125–126|ps=, and others.}} moreover, modern definitions of the word {{lang|la|abacus}} universally describe it as a frame with rods and beads{{sfn|American Heritage|2004|ps=, s.v. "abacus"}} and, in general, do not include the definition of "sand table".

The sand table may well have been the predecessor to some [[board games]]. ("The word {{tlit|ar|abax}}, or abacus, is used both for the reckoning-board with its counters and the play-board with its pieces, {{omission}}").{{sfn|Tylor|1879|p=234}} {{tlit|grc|Abax}} is from the [[Old Greek#Evolution from Ancient to Modern Greek|old Greek]] for "sand table".{{sfn|American Heritage|2004|ps=, s.v. "abacus"}}

== Ghubār ==
{{further info|Ghubār numerals}}

An Arabic word for sand (or dust) is {{tlit|ar|ghubār}} (or {{tlit|ar|gubar}}), and Western numerals (the [[decimal]] digits 0&ndash;9) are derived from the style of digits written on dust boards (or {{tlit|ar|takht}}) in North-West Africa and Iberia, also described as the 'West Arabic' or '{{tlit|ar|ghubār}}' style.<ref>{{cite book |last1=O'Connor |first1=J. J. |first2=E. F. |last2=Robertson |date=2001 |title=The Arabic numeral system |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Arabic_numerals/ |publisher=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]]}}</ref>

== Military use ==
[[File:Exercise Desert Punch Marine sand table 2.gif|thumb|Marines view a sand table model of the operating area of [[Exercise Desert Punch]] constructed on the desert floor near [[Yuma, Arizona]]]]

Sand tables have been used for [[military plan]]ning and [[wargaming]] for many years as a field expedient, [[Scale (map)|small-scale map]], and in [[Military training|training]] for [[Battle|military actions]]. In 1890 a Sand table room was built at the [[Royal Military College of Canada]] for use in teaching cadets military tactics; this replaced the old sand table room in a pre-college building, in which the weight of the sand had damaged the floor.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Preston |first=Richard |title=Canada's RMC: A History of the Royal Military College |publisher=University of Toronto Press |location=Toronto |date=1969}}</ref> The use of sand tables increasingly fell out of favour with improved maps, aerial and satellite photography, and later, with digital terrain simulations. More modern sand tables have incorporated [[Augmented reality|Augmented Reality]], such as the [[Augmented Reality Sandtable (ARES)]] developed by the [[United States Army Research Laboratory|Army Research Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-armys-new-projection-mapped-sandtable/ |title=Design Digital Terrain with the Army's Projection-Mapped Sandtable |last=Mufson |first=Beckett |date=5 November 2014 |work=Vice Creators |access-date=2 August 2018}}</ref> Today, virtual and conventional sand tables are used in operations training.

In 1991, "Special Forces teams discovered an elaborate sand-table model of the Iraqi military plan for the defense of Kuwait City. Four huge red arrows from the sea pointed at the coastline of Kuwait City and the huge defensive effort positioned there. Small fences of concertina wire marked the shoreline and models of artillery pieces lined the shore area. Throughout the city were plastic models of other artillery and air defense positions, while thin, red-painted strips of board designated supply routes and main highways."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/inatl/longterm/iraq/timeline/022891.htm |title=Arab Forces, Marines Take Kuwait City |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=28 February 1991}}</ref>

In 2006, [[Google Earth]] users looking at satellite photography of China found a several ''kilometre'' large "sand table" scale model, strikingly reminiscent of a mountainous region ([[Aksai Chin]]) which China occupies militarily in a disputed zone with India, 2400&nbsp;km from the model's location. Speculation has been rife that the terrain is used for military exercises of familiarisation.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.smh.com.au/news/web/chinese-xfile-excites-spotters/2006/07/20/1153166503699.html |title=Chinese X-file excites spotters |newspaper=[[Sydney Morning Herald]] |date=20 July 2006}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.indianexpress.com/news/from-sky-see-how-china-builds-model-of-indian-border-2400-km-away/9972/ |title=From sky, see how China builds model of Indian border 2400 km away |newspaper=[[The Indian Express]] |date=4 August 2006}}</ref>

== Education ==

A sand table is a device useful for teaching in the [[Educational stages|early grades]] and for [[Special education|special needs children]].{{sfn|Raines|Canady|1992|p=101}}{{sfn|Wagner|1999|p=80}}
